Quick Read

Nvidia plunged as much as 13% after Jensen Huang resigned, yet QQQ slid just 0.58% because Nvidia makes up only about 8% of the fund.

Narrower funds take far bigger hits: Nvidia fills about 15% of XLK and 18% of SMH, so selloffs hurt them more than QQQ.

Holding QQQ, XLK, SMH and an S&P 500 fund stacks Nvidia exposure, so portfolios that look diversified can carry hidden concentration.

Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) shares were down 5.01% at $165.03 as of 10:29 AM ET on Thursday, after Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive. Axios reported that the stock fell as much as 13% after the news and then recovered some of that loss. Investors who hold Nvidia through the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) took a much smaller hit, because of how little of the fund Nvidia makes up.

24/7 Wall St.
NVDA Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.
Inside Nvidia's Leadership Shake-Up

Per Axios, Nvidia's board named longtime CFO Colette Kress interim CEO and started a search for a permanent replacement. Axios reported that Nvidia did not give a reason for the resignation. The departure follows press reports about Huang's personal relationships. Axios noted that The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang had a relationship with a senior Nvidia executive who reports to him.

Axios also reported that on Nov. 8, Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation after reports that Huang may have been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. The New York Times reported that U.S. officials believed a businesswoman with close ties to Huang was gathering intelligence for Beijing.

In a note to staff quoted by Axios, Kress wrote: "I believe deeply in this company and in its future." According to the same report, the board expects operations, customer commitments and the product roadmap to continue without interruption.

title: History Shows the QQQ ETF Could Plunge 50%-70%, But Modern Investors Have New Tools to Protect Themselves and Still Profit
detail:
History Shows the QQQ ETF Could Plunge 50%-70%, But Modern Investors Have New Tools to Protect Themselves and Still Profit
Rob Isbitts
Thu, November 12, 2026 at 8:43 AM MST 3 min read
QQQ
Trade QQQ on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
A concept image of a lit bomb by Leigh Prather via Shutterstock

The average retail investor knows how good the stock market can be. They DO NOT know how bad it can get.

The Invesco QQQ ETF (QQQ) fell 70% from its peak during the dot-com era. It then fell more than 50% from its peak during the Global Financial Crisis. I'm going to guess that no more than 20% of the people reading this are aware of that.

More News from Barchart

Dear SpaceX Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for November 13

Oracle Stock Just Scored a New $325 Price Target

Nvidia Stock Plunges After Hours as Reports of a Second Jensen Huang Relationship Could Force the CEO Out

Tired of missing midday reversals? The FREE Barchart Brief newsletter keeps you in the know. Sign up now!

Not because you didn't experience it. You didn't have to. Instead, it's because investors are not taught what markets are capable of on the downside.

Human nature is to buy stocks, see them go up, and buy more whenever they drop. That has worked for the better part of 18 years. We've had a few quick drops in the stock market, but each time the recovery was a letter "V," not a letter "U."

For the Qs, It's All About the U

Those longer, U-shaped recoveries are what alter retirements. We might not see one for a long time. Or, we might be in the beginning stages of one.

The question is, do you care? I think most investors absolutely should care. But do they? I suspect not. They are too used to things working out in their favor.

Chart submitted by Rob Isbitts

That's why I think this chart above is important to familiarize yourself with. To simply stare at it and say "that won't happen again" is like saying bond rates will never go to 5% again. Or, when Bitcoin (BTCUSD) crossed above $100,000, concluding it could never drop back down to five digits.

The chart above shows the last four months of 2000. Here's 2026 by comparison, including Monday's surge.

Chart submitted by Rob Isbitts

During the last four months of 2000, you could have bought the dip 15 times. And each time, QQQ, headed lower. Think about that for a moment.

I am not predicting the future here. I'm just defining in plain language what we technicians call a "downtrend." The problem I see these days is that investors are very quick to call "the bottom." Investing is really about what happens not at the extremes, but over time.

Keep in mind what QQQ is, what's on its resume, and what we just experienced via the AI trade. Bubble or no? Wrong question! Prepare for anything? That's my preference.

I continue to emphasize active use of inverse ETFs like the ProShares Short QQQ (PSQ), ProShares UltraShort QQQ ETF (QID), and the ProShares UltraPro Short QQQ (SQQQ), which are single, double, and triple the reverse direction of QQQ. I use a lot of put options on QQQ as well, but when option volatility spikes, those get expensive quickly.

title: Jensen Huang Resigns from NVIDIA, Shares -10%
detail:
Jensen Huang Resigns from NVIDIA, Shares -10%
Mark Vickery
Thu, November 12, 2026 at 7:12 AM MST 3 min read
NVDA
^IXIC
^GSPC
^RUT
QQQ
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Thursday, November 12th, 2026

Pre-market futures are back in the red somewhat this morning, with the bond market re-engaged after Wednesday's bank holiday, and as the tech world grapples with the concept of a Jensen Huang-less NVIDIA NVDA. Shares of the (until recently) world's largest company by market cap is down another -8.6% this morning. The Dow is presently -249 points, the Nasdaq is -445, the S&P 500 is -66 and the small-cap Russell 2000 is -23 points at this hour.

Bond yields are back up over +5% on both the 10-year and 30-year this morning: +5.056 and +5.395%, while the 2-year yield is +4.818%. These figures have tightened their yield curves, as well — all are well within the "normal" 40 basis-point (bps) gap. The yields jumped within seconds of President Trump issuing a notice that the U.S. does "not need a deal with Iran." 

Initial Jobless Claims Reach 200K


A new report on Initial Jobless Claims for last week came up to +200K exactly — breaking a long string of sub-200K claims going back to Labor Day. This follows the slightly upwardly revised +191K the previous week. Even at +200K, we are looking at very healthy employment numbers from this angle.

Continuing Claims, reported a week in arrears, came in sub-1.7 million this morning: +1.697 million, from a slight downward revision to +1.717 million the prior week. Again, we're seeing historically few Americans filing jobless claims, as has been the case for  couple months now. 

However, strong employment figures — such as the ones we saw during Jobs Week last week — remove a possible hindrance to the Fed raising interest rates to curb inflation. Full employment is the other half of the Fed's mandate, but these numbers do reflect a scenario very close to full employment.

What to Expect from the Stock Market Today


News headlines are coming across: CEO Jensen Huang is stepping down immediately from his post as Chairman and CEO of NVIDIA. The company's CFO, Colette Kress, has been named interim CEO, with the company looking for a permanent search for a replacement to Huang, who is the only CEO NVIDIA has ever had. This news will suck much of the air out of today's market sentiment.

Elsewhere, Existing Home Sales for October are expected at 10am ET this morning. Estimates are for another downward tick, to 3.8K seasonally adjusted, annualized units from 3.99K reported a month ago. Housing has been rough sledding for nearly four years. The recent low was in August: +3.93K, while the recent high was December at +4.27K. Until interest rates make mortgages more accommodative, expect these woes to continue.

We'll also hear from Fed members today, including Fed Governor Michael Barr, San Francisco President Mary Daly and New York President John Williams. Analysts will be checking to see if any or all of these members are in-line with Fed Governor Chris Waller and Dallas President Lorie Logan, who sounded open to a 50-bps hike at its December meeting.
